title: Isaac Born, Ishmael Sent Away, a Well Secured
summary: The LORD keeps his word, and Sarah bears Isaac to Abraham in their old age. At Isaac's weaning feast Sarah sees Ishmael mocking and demands that Hagar and her son be sent away; God tells Abraham to listen, and then rescues the dying boy in the wilderness. Abraham makes a sworn treaty with Abimelech at Beersheba and calls on the name of the LORD, the Eternal God.
story: Twenty-five years after the first promise (Genesis 12:4), the son arrives. Everything since Genesis 12 has been leaning toward this birth, and the chapter opens by insisting that it happened exactly “as He had said” and “at the very time God had promised.” But the birth of the promised son also brings the tension in Abraham's household to a head, and Ishmael and Hagar leave for good, carried by their own promise from God. The chapter ends with Abraham gaining a legal right to a well in the land, a small first foothold in the territory his descendants will one day possess. The next chapter will put the long-awaited son on an altar.
historical:
Beersheba lies in the northern Negev, where wells were the key to life for herders. The mound of Tel Beersheba, excavated from 1969 under Yohanan Aharoni, is mainly an Iron Age town, later than the period usually assigned to Abraham; Genesis doesn't picture a city here but herdsmen digging and disputing wells in open country. Paran (verse 21) is the wilderness of the northeastern Sinai, south of Canaan.

Genesis 21:32-34 speaks of the land of the Philistines. The Philistines known from archaeology and later biblical books settled on the southern coast of Canaan in the twelfth century BC, well after the time usually given for Abraham. Interpreters explain this in different ways: that the narrator uses a later, familiar name for the region, much as we might speak of ancient Paris; that earlier Aegean groups were already present in the area; or that the stories were shaped in a later period. Abimelech and Phicol in any case appear here as a local king and his commander dealing with a powerful herdsman.
cultural:
Children in the ancient Near East were usually weaned at around two or three years old, and given how many infants died, reaching weaning was a milestone worth a feast. Sarah's demand has a legal background. The laws of Hammurabi provided that the sons of a slave woman could share an inheritance if their father had formally acknowledged them as his children; if he had not, they did not inherit, but the woman and her children were to be set free. Sarah insists that Ishmael will not share the inheritance with Isaac. Sending him away, painful as it is, also releases Hagar and Ishmael from slavery.

The treaty with Abimelech shows how disputes over water were settled. Abraham gives seven ewe lambs as a witness that he dug the well, and the two swear an oath. The name Beersheba holds a double wordplay, since in Hebrew seven and swear sound alike: it can mean well of seven or well of the oath. Planting a tamarisk, a hardy, long-lived desert tree, marked the place and made a claim of settled presence.
literary: The chapter has three scenes: Isaac's birth (verses 1-7), Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness (verses 8-21), and the treaty at Beersheba (verses 22-34). Laughter runs through the first two. Isaac's name means he laughs; Sarah says, “God has made me laugh”; and in verse 9 Ishmael is literally laughing (the same root), which translations render as mocking or playing. The desert scene closely mirrors Genesis 16: Hagar in the wilderness, water, the angel's call, a promise of a great nation, and God's attention to the one who cries out. It also anticipates Genesis 22, where another father sets out early in the morning, another son is near death, and an angel calls from heaven. The two sons of Abraham both come to the edge of death and are both saved.

outline.t: Isaac is born, and Sarah laughs
Sarah demands that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away
God hears the boy in the wilderness
Abraham's treaty with Abimelech at Beersheba

doctrines.note: God keeps his word on his schedule, “at the very time God had promised” (verse 2). He also watches over Ishmael, who is outside the covenant line: “God was with the boy” (verse 20). His care is not limited to the chosen line.

God tells Abraham that “through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned” (verse 12). The covenant line is defined by God's promise, not simply by being Abraham's biological son. The treaty with Abimelech shows covenants between people, sealed by oath and witness, as part of ordinary life.
Abraham calls on “the LORD, the Eternal God” (verse 33). The title El Olam, found only here in Genesis, names God as the one whose life spans every age and who keeps his promises across generations.

words.note: Paqad, to visit, attend to, take note of, or appoint. When God visits someone in the Old Testament it can mean blessing or judgment. Here “the LORD attended to Sarah” (verse 1): God turns his attention to her to act on what he promised. Joseph will use the same verb when he says God will surely visit his people and bring them out of Egypt (Genesis 50:24).

Shava, to swear an oath. The verb shares its sound with sheva, seven, which explains the seven ewe lambs and the name Beersheba. An oath in the ancient world called God to witness and punish falsehood, which is why Abimelech asks Abraham to swear “before God.”

Olam, a long duration, forever, ancient or everlasting. Joined with El, God, it names the Eternal God. In the Old Testament the word stresses unending duration more than philosophical timelessness: this God was there before Abraham and will be there after all his descendants.

christ: The New Testament draws on this chapter in several places. Paul quotes God's word to Abraham, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,” in Romans 9:7 to show that belonging to God's people is a matter of promise, not merely descent. In Galatians 4:28-31 he reads the two sons figuratively: believers, like Isaac, are “children of promise,” born by the Spirit, and he quotes Sarah's words about the slave woman and her son. Hebrews 11:18 recalls the same promise as the background to Abraham's test in Genesis 22. Isaac's birth to a woman long past childbearing, by God's word and at God's appointed time, belongs to a line of miraculous births (Samson, Samuel, John the Baptist) that reaches its height in the virgin birth of Jesus. That last link is a pattern the Gospels invite rather than a prophecy Genesis states.

hard.q: Does God approve of Sarah's demand to drive out Hagar and Ishmael?
hard.a:
The scene is painful, and the text doesn't hide it. Sarah's words are harsh, and Abraham is deeply distressed. God tells Abraham to listen to Sarah, but the reason he gives is not that Sarah is right in her attitude. It is that the covenant line will run through Isaac, while Ishmael will also become a nation “because he is your offspring” (verse 13). God affirms the outcome, the separation of the two lines, and then personally ensures that Hagar and Ishmael survive and flourish. The legal background also matters: sent away rather than sold, they left as free people.

A smaller puzzle is Ishmael's age. He was fourteen when Isaac was born and older at the weaning, yet verses 14-16 can sound as if he were a small child placed on Hagar's shoulder and left under a bush. The Hebrew of verse 14 can be read as putting only the bread and water on her shoulder, and the word for boy covers a wide range of ages; a teenager dying of thirst could well be laid in the shade by his mother. Readers differ on how to weigh these details, but the story's point is clear: God hears the voice of the boy.

questions: Sarah waited decades for this laughter. How do you hold on to a promise over a long wait without either giving up or forcing it?
God heard Ishmael and cared for Hagar even though the covenant line ran through Isaac. What does that say about God's attention to people outside the center of the story?
Abraham secured a small, legal foothold in the land with a well and a tree. What small, faithful acts might be signs of a larger hope in your life?
